messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 18
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: Oceania
  relationship_status: In a relationship
  occupation: Project Manager
  trauma_type: Witnessed domestic violence (childhood)
  pcl5: 55

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Male Presence: Being alone with men, Transportation (Bicycle): Bicycle, Olfactory (Alcohol): Alcohol smell
  Maladaptive Strategies: Smoking: I smoke, Substance Use: I drink alcohol, take medication or use drugs, Avoid People: avoid other people
  Threat: Door and Lock Checking: I repeatedly check that doors and windows are locked, Startle to Sounds: I jump or startle at ordinary sounds that would not bother most people, Watching Others: I watch other people closely for signs that they might harm me
  Memory: Incomplete Picture: I feel like I am only remembering parts of what happened and the rest is missing, Terror on Recall: Remembering the event brings back the same terror I felt at the time, Fragmented Pieces: My memories of the event come in disconnected pieces that do not fit together

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Rangi Tuilagi is an eighteen-year-old Samoan-American male who presents for his initial intake following a referral from his university's student health service. He works part-time as a junior project manager at a small construction consultancy, a role that places him regularly in the company of older men on job sites and in site offices. He is currently in a romantic relationship, though he reports that his partner has grown increasingly concerned about changes in his behaviour over recent months. His PCL-5 score of 55 places him firmly within the severe range of post-traumatic stress symptomatology.

Rangi grew up in a household in which his father's drinking was a fixed and threatening constant. What he describes, haltingly and in fragments across the first two sessions, is less a single event than a sustained landscape of fear — though one night in particular appears to anchor much of what he now carries. He was around seven years old. He remembers the smell first: the sharp, sweet-sour odour of alcohol that would drift under his bedroom door and tell him, before he heard anything, what kind of night it was going to be. Then the sound of his father's bicycle being dropped against the front steps. Then his mother's voice, low and placating, and then the impact of something — he cannot say what — and her cry. He recalls pressing himself into the corner behind his bed, watching the strip of light under the door. The rest, he says, is missing. He does not know how the night ended. He does not know how he got to school the next morning. What remains are those pieces — the smell, the sound of the bicycle, the light under the door — vivid and unordered, surfacing without warning and carrying with them the same paralysing terror he felt as a small boy in the dark.

In the years since, Rangi finished high school with strong grades and moved into work earlier than most of his peers. On the surface he appeared capable and self-possessed. But the fragments never organised themselves into a coherent past. Remembering does not feel like remembering — it feels, he says, like being dropped back into that hallway, heart hammering, certain that something terrible is still about to happen.

At the consultancy, his days require him to attend morning briefings in small site offices with male colleagues and subcontractors. He has come to watch the men around him with a careful, exhausting vigilance — noting who raises their voice, who stands too close, who smells of last night's drinking. When a senior colleague arrived at a Tuesday briefing with alcohol on his breath, Rangi left the room on a fabricated errand and did not return. His manager has noted his absences. Riding his bicycle to the office, which he does most mornings, has become a source of dread he cannot fully explain to himself — there is something about the particular sound of tyres on gravel, or the act of leaning the frame against a wall, that causes his chest to tighten before he has even reached the door. He has begun locking his apartment compulsively each evening, checking the door handle four or five times before he can sit down, and again before he sleeps. Ordinary sounds — a door slamming in the corridor, a raised voice from a neighbouring flat — cause him to startle badly enough that his partner has started warning him before she enters a room.

To manage the edges of all this, Rangi smokes heavily and drinks most evenings, aware of the irony and troubled by it. He has also begun avoiding social gatherings, withdrawing from a friendship group he valued through his final year of school. His partner, who does not yet know the full shape of what happened in his childhood, has told him she feels shut out.

What finally brought him to the student health service was a performance review in which his manager raised concerns about reliability. Rangi had worked hard for this role and had come to believe that his competence was the one thing that could not be taken from him. The possibility that the past might cost him that too was, he said quietly, more than he could sit with alone. What he hopes for, most of all, is to understand why the pieces will not fit together — and whether they ever could.
